author: Stefan Redlich
title: First of all, Happy New Year everybody! 2017 has been a spe
text:
First of all, Happy New Year everybody!

2017 has been a special year with global stock markets, particularly the US markets, rallying strongly. The broad S&P 500 (NYSEARCA: SPY ) almost gained 20% and was outperformed significantly by the Dow Jones (+25%) and the tech-heavy Nasdaq (+32%).
SPY data by YCharts Overall, it has been a banner year for US stocks and with the corporate tax reform having been finalized just before the beginning of the new year, a big catalyst for stocks in 2018 is gaining momentum.
My personal portfolio performance in 2017 was much lower though (+9% in EUR, my home currency, and +15% in USD). The euro appreciated irritatingly strongly against the dollar in 2017 posting a 13% gain. As my portfolio is heavily weighted towards US stocks, the strong euro has diminished both my portfolio performance and my dividend income in home currency. Although I really do not understand why the euro is rising against the US dollar given that the interest differential across the two economic regions clearly points to a stronger US dollar, I am not concerned about this. I am playing the long game and in that game these exchange rate fluctuations will not really matter.
I am still working on developing a proper tool to easily monitor and track FX impact and portfolio performance for current and prior years but this is taking longer than expected. I am hoping to have it finished for my January 2018 update in order to share better metrics with you.
Portfolio Changes | 3 new stocks, several sales and 20 repurchases Heavy buying and partially selling took place in December. I spent around $4,350 for buying stock and sold stocks worth $1,870 resulting in net capital deployed of $2,480.
I sold out my stake in Total ( TOT ) and redeployed these funds into British Petroleum ( BP ) and Spectra Energy Partners ( SEP ), as both offer a better yield and faster growth. I also exited my positions in Chatham Lodging Trust ( CLDT ) and Hospitality Properties Trust ( HPT ) and redeployed the capital into Senior Housing Properties ( SNH ) in order to better consolidate my holdings and reducing tiny positions.
I also trimmed Apple ( AAPL ) and McDonald's ( MCD ) slightly in order to realize some gains which I invested back into Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce ( CM ), which is the highest-yielding Canadian bank within the Big Five and a superb dividend growth stock fairly valued.
Other main purchases break down as follows:
1) Continue ongoing monthly stock savings plans : These are routine investments between $50-115 each into Wells Fargo ( WFC ), Visa ( V ), McDonald's ( MCD ), Johnson & Johnson ( JNJ ), Apple ( AAPL ) and the lesser known Commonwealth Bank of Australia ( OTCPK:CBAUF ).
2) Invest in existing growth stocks: I added to Dominion Energy ( D ) once it hiked its dividend by a staggering 10%, Bank of America ( BAC ), Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Honeywell ( HON ), a software industrial giant which has enjoyed a stellar run in 2017, is firing on all cylinders and is also priced at the high end of the valuation spectrum. Despite that high valuation I added to my position as double-digit dividend and earnings growth will prove decisive over the long-term. Honeywell's outlook for 2018 is very solid and the success story should continue in 2018 as well.
3) Invest in existing dividend stocks: I added more shares to my already large AT&T ( T ) stake as the stock moved into the $39 price region yet again. A yield of around 5% is more than sufficient for me to weather continued price pressure on the stock as the company is transforming its entire business. I am in it for income and do not expect any capital appreciation unless the Time Warner ( TWX ) merger gets completely cancelled and AT&T decides to invest this money otherwise. Similarly, I added to Southern Company ( SO ) when the stock hit the $47.5 price region, although in hindsight that was a bit too early given that it now trades in the low $45s fueled by rising treasury yields.
4) Speculative buys: I bought a few shares in Uniti Group ( UNIT ) motivated by fellow SA authors and the stock's dividend yield. For similar reasons I also invested a bit into Macquarie Infrastructure ( MIC ), a high-yield stock with fantastic dividend growth that has been beaten down in 2017. And finally I bought two shares of Galapagos ( GLPG ) in speculation of Gilead ( GILD ) or another biotech or pharma company using the expiration of the lock-out period to buy a meaningful stake in Galapagos.
All purchases and sales in December can be found below:

Dividend Income: What happened on the dividend side? My income from 31 corporations amounted to $205.6 in dividends, up 12% sequentially and 54% Y/Y. 
In December 56% of total dividend income originated from five companies, spearheaded by Royal Dutch Shell ( RDS.B ), one of my best stock investments over the last two years. Due to several purchases in 2017 dividend income from Gilead has reached second spot in December and is expected grow with double-digit pace in the coming years. Once the stock leaves its multi-year bear market trend, I am expecting strong capital appreciation here and there are a lot of signs that 2018 could be that year (HIV market launch in China, more strategic focus on strongly growing HIV business, tax reform and potentially more acquisitions are key catalysts here).

This dashboard shows how the monthly dividend income breaks down into the individual stocks. It also shows the change in income vs. the previous quarter and year.
Here is a look at my favorite chart, the net dividend income development by month over time between 2015 and 2017, where you can easily see the development of my dividend income as well as the average annual dividend in a given year:

Next, I have scattered all the individual dividend payments I have ever received and colored them by year:

For December we can clearly detect the big payment from Shell. It also clearly shows how unevenly dividend income was distributed in December compared to other months and how that progressed since I started my journey. For better readability I split and color-coded the horizontal axis by year while still using the same scaling for the three years. I just cherish this development and could not be happier about it.
It will be fascinating to watch how all these metrics develop over time. Right now, as I am still in the early stages, these metrics are not that impressive but the growth is truly striking and all these instruments help me measure it and provide meaning to it.
Speaking in terms of meaning, another way to express the monthly dividend income is in terms of Gifted Working Time (GWT). I am assuming an average hourly rate of $20 here.

What this shows is the following...
1) All-time (blue area): Around 139 hours or more than 17 days of active work have been replaced with passive income since the start of my dividend journey. Assuming a 5-day work week that equals more than three weeks of vacation funded via dividends.
